lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Biochemistry foundations: energy, groups, and bonds
lessons.subtitle: The chemical grammar behind every later pathway
topicPatterns: Metabolism, ATP, functional groups, and bonds

visual.caption: Connect molecular structure to energy use and biological function.

items.label: Matter
items.detail: CHNOPS atoms are arranged into carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids.

items.label: Functional groups
items.detail: Hydroxyl and carbonyl groups add polarity; carboxyl groups donate H+; amino groups accept H+; phosphate transfers energy; sulfhydryls form disulfides.

items.label: Catabolism
items.detail: Large molecules are oxidized to smaller products, releasing energy captured mainly as ATP and reduced cofactors.

items.label: Anabolism
items.detail: Small precursors are assembled into complex molecules using ATP and usually NADPH.

items.label: Information
items.detail: DNA is transcribed into RNA, and coding RNA is translated into protein.

essentials: ATP hydrolysis drives unfavorable reactions by coupling; ATP is an energy-transfer currency, not long-term energy storage.
Covalent bonds build molecules; hydrogen bonds, ionic attractions, van der Waals forces, and hydrophobic interactions control folding and recognition.
Oxidation is loss of electrons or hydrogen; reduction is gain of electrons or hydrogen.
Amphipathic molecules contain both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions and can self-assemble into membranes.

traps.wrong: Anabolism produces ATP by breaking molecules down.
traps.right: Catabolism releases usable energy; anabolism consumes it to synthesize molecules.

traps.wrong: Hydrophobic interactions are covalent bonds between nonpolar groups.
traps.right: They are noncovalent clustering effects driven by exclusion of nonpolar surfaces from water.

recognition: A phosphate-containing energy-transfer reaction usually points to ATP coupling.
Two cysteine side chains linked together identify a disulfide bond.

source.label: TUMS Biochemistry Introduction + Lippincott
source.detail: INTRODUCTION.ppt, slides 3–31; Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, foundational chemistry cross-check.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Water, osmosis, and body-fluid compartments
lessons.subtitle: Where water sits and what makes it move

visual.caption: Total body water divides first into ICF and ECF, then ECF into interstitial fluid and plasma.

items.label: Total body water
items.detail: About 60% of body weight in a typical lean adult male, lower with more adipose tissue and often lower in females and older adults.

items.label: ICF
items.detail: About two-thirds of total body water; K+, Mg2+, phosphate, and proteins predominate.

items.label: ECF
items.detail: About one-third of total body water; Na+, Cl−, and bicarbonate predominate.

items.label: Interstitial fluid
items.detail: Roughly three-quarters of ECF, outside cells and outside the vascular compartment.

items.label: Plasma
items.detail: Roughly one-quarter of ECF; plasma proteins create colloid osmotic pressure.

essentials: Water is polar and forms hydrogen bonds, giving it strong solvent, thermal, and cohesive properties.
Water moves across a semipermeable membrane toward the compartment with higher effective osmolarity.
At equilibrium, ICF and ECF osmolarities are nearly equal even though their ion compositions differ.
An amphipathic molecule has a polar region and a nonpolar region; membrane lipids are the central example.

traps.wrong: Most extracellular fluid is plasma.
traps.right: Most ECF is interstitial fluid; plasma is the smaller ECF subdivision.

traps.wrong: Water moves toward lower solute concentration.
traps.right: Water moves toward higher effective solute concentration until osmotic equilibrium.

recognition: A compartment rich in Na+ and Cl− is ECF; one rich in K+ and phosphate is ICF.
A molecule drawn with a charged head and hydrocarbon tail is amphipathic.

source.label: TUMS Water and Buffer + Marks
source.detail: Water and Buffer 1404.ppt, slides 3–8; Marks’ Water, Acids, Bases, and Buffers reference, pp. 21–24.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.topic: pH, acids, bases, Ka, and pKa
lessons.title: pH, weak acids, Ka, and pKa
lessons.subtitle: Read acid strength and protonation without guessing
topicPatterns: pH, acids, bases, Ka, and pKa

visual.caption: pKa ranks acid strength; the difference between pH and pKa predicts protonation.

items.label: Strong acid
items.detail: Dissociates almost completely in water; large Ka and low pKa.

items.label: Weak acid
items.detail: Partially dissociates and establishes HA ⇌ H+ + A−; smaller Ka and higher pKa.

items.label: pH < pKa
items.detail: The environment is relatively proton-rich, so HA predominates.

items.label: pH = pKa
items.detail: Concentrations of HA and A− are equal.

items.label: pH > pKa
items.detail: The environment is relatively proton-poor, so A− predominates.

essentials: pH = −log[H+]; a one-unit pH change is a tenfold change in hydrogen-ion concentration.
At 25°C, pH + pOH = 14 for dilute aqueous solutions.
Ka measures dissociation directly; pKa = −log Ka, so stronger acids have lower pKa values.
An acid donates H+ and its conjugate base is what remains; a base accepts H+.

traps.wrong: A higher pKa means a stronger acid.
traps.right: A lower pKa means a stronger acid because Ka is larger.

traps.wrong: At pH = pKa the acid is completely dissociated.
traps.right: At pH = pKa, protonated and deprotonated forms are present in equal amounts.

recognition: If pH is two units above pKa, the deprotonated form exceeds the protonated form by 100:1.
A titration midpoint marks pH = pKa.

source.label: TUMS Water and Buffer
source.detail: Water and Buffer 1404.ppt, slides 9–20; teacher definitions and pH/Ka/pKa examples.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Titration curves and buffer capacity
lessons.subtitle: Turn a curve into ratios, pKa, and buffer strength

visual.caption: Follow a weak acid as base is added: acid-rich → maximum buffering → base-rich → equivalence.

items.label: Start
items.detail: Mostly HA is present; pH is below pKa and added base converts HA to A−.

items.label: Buffer region
items.detail: Both HA and A− are appreciable; effective buffering is approximately pKa ± 1 pH unit.

items.label: Half-equivalence
items.detail: Half the acid has been converted to conjugate base, so [A−] = [HA] and pH = pKa.

items.label: Toward equivalence
items.detail: A− increasingly predominates and the curve rises more steeply as buffer reserve is exhausted.

items.label: Equivalence
items.detail: Stoichiometric neutralization is complete; this is not the same point as half-equivalence.

essentials: Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA]).
A tenfold increase in [A−]/[HA] raises pH by one unit.
Buffer capacity is greatest when pH is near pKa and rises with total buffer concentration.
Choose a buffer with a pKa near the desired working pH.

traps.wrong: Maximum buffering occurs at the equivalence point.
traps.right: Maximum buffering occurs near half-equivalence, where pH = pKa and HA equals A−.

traps.wrong: Diluting a buffer changes its acid-to-base ratio and therefore always changes pH greatly.
traps.right: Ideal dilution preserves the ratio and pH approximately, but lowers buffer capacity.

recognition: The flattest central region of a weak-acid titration curve is the buffer region.
The point where half the titrant required for equivalence has been added reveals pKa.

source.label: TUMS Water and Buffer + Titration practical
source.detail: Water and Buffer 1404.ppt, slides 22–28; Titration Esmaeili Jan 2026.pdf, pp. 1–10.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Physiological buffers: bicarbonate, phosphate, and proteins
lessons.subtitle: Match each buffer to its compartment and controller

visual.caption: Body pH is protected immediately by buffers, then by lungs, then by kidneys.

items.label: Bicarbonate
items.detail: Major extracellular system: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−; lungs control CO2 and kidneys control HCO3−.

items.label: Hemoglobin
items.detail: Deoxyhemoglobin accepts H+ produced when CO2 is hydrated in RBCs; oxygenation in lungs promotes H+ release and CO2 exhalation.

items.label: Plasma proteins
items.detail: Ionizable amino-acid side chains, especially histidine, accept or donate protons.

items.label: Phosphate
items.detail: HPO4²−/H2PO4− is most useful intracellularly and in renal tubular fluid because concentration and pH suit its pKa.

items.label: Controllers
items.detail: Chemical buffers act in seconds, ventilation in minutes, and renal net acid excretion over hours to days.

essentials: Clinical bicarbonate equation: pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3−]/(0.03 × PCO2)).
Bicarbonate works well despite a pKa below blood pH because CO2 is continuously regulated by the lungs.
The chloride shift exchanges HCO3− and Cl− across the RBC membrane to transport large amounts of CO2 as bicarbonate.
Respiratory changes alter the denominator; metabolic or renal changes chiefly alter bicarbonate in the numerator.

traps.wrong: Phosphate is the quantitatively dominant extracellular buffer.
traps.right: Bicarbonate is the major extracellular buffer; phosphate is more important intracellularly and in urine.

traps.wrong: Oxyhemoglobin binds H+ better than deoxyhemoglobin.
traps.right: Deoxyhemoglobin is the better H+ buffer; oxygenation favors proton release in the lungs.

recognition: A question pairing lungs with CO2 and kidneys with bicarbonate is testing the open bicarbonate system.
Urinary buffering by HPO4²− to H2PO4− identifies titratable acid.

source.label: TUMS Water and Buffer + Marks
source.detail: Water and Buffer 1404.ppt, slides 29–35; Marks reference pp. 26–28.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Water-soluble vitamins: coenzymes and deficiency signatures
lessons.subtitle: Match the active form to the reaction and clinical clue

visual.caption: Use one anchor for each vitamin: active coenzyme → reaction class → deficiency clue.

items.label: B1, B2, B3
items.detail: B1/TPP transfers aldehyde units in oxidative decarboxylation and transketolase; B2/FAD-FMN and B3/NAD-NADP carry electrons.

items.label: B5, B6, B7
items.detail: B5 is part of CoA/acyl transfer; B6/PLP handles amino-acid reactions and heme synthesis; biotin carries CO2 in carboxylation.

items.label: B9 folate
items.detail: THF carries one-carbon units for purines and thymidylate; deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia without neurologic deficits.

items.label: B12 cobalamin
items.detail: Required for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia plus neurologic injury and elevated methylmalonate.

items.label: Vitamin C
items.detail: Reduces iron and supports proline/lysine hydroxylation in collagen; deficiency causes bleeding, poor wound healing, and corkscrew hairs.

essentials: Most water-soluble vitamins act as coenzyme precursors and have limited stores; B12 is the major exception with substantial hepatic stores.
B1 deficiency produces beriberi or Wernicke–Korsakoff; pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain dehydrogenase, and transketolase require TPP.
B3 can be synthesized from tryptophan; deficiency causes pellagra: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, and potentially death.
B6 deficiency can cause neuropathy, seizures, cheilosis, and sideroblastic anemia; isoniazid increases risk.
Folate can correct B12-deficient anemia while neurologic damage progresses, so distinguish them before treatment.

traps.wrong: Folate deficiency raises methylmalonic acid.
traps.right: Methylmalonic acid rises in B12 deficiency; homocysteine may rise in either B12 or folate deficiency.

traps.wrong: Biotin is used by decarboxylases.
traps.right: Biotin carries activated CO2 for carboxylases.

recognition: Megaloblastic anemia plus neurologic findings points to B12 rather than isolated folate deficiency.
Bleeding gums and poor wound healing identify vitamin C deficiency.
Confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia in malnutrition suggest B1 deficiency.

source.label: TUMS Vitamin lecture + Lippincott
source.detail: Vitamin 2024.pdf, pp. 4–45; Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, Chapter 28.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K
lessons.subtitle: Absorption, storage, function, deficiency, and toxicity

visual.caption: ADEK travel with fat, so malabsorption can impair all four and storage makes toxicity more likely.

items.label: A
items.detail: Retinal supports vision; retinoic acid controls epithelial differentiation and gene transcription. Deficiency: night blindness and xerophthalmia.

items.label: D
items.detail: Activated by liver 25-hydroxylation then kidney 1α-hydroxylation; calcitriol raises intestinal Ca2+ and phosphate absorption.

items.label: E
items.detail: Lipid-phase antioxidant protecting membranes from peroxidation. Deficiency: hemolysis and neurologic dysfunction.

items.label: K
items.detail: Cofactor for γ-carboxylation of glutamate in factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S, enabling Ca2+ binding.

essentials: Fat-soluble vitamin absorption requires normal fat digestion, bile delivery, micelles, and chylomicron formation.
Vitamin D activation is stimulated by PTH at the renal 1α-hydroxylase step; deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.
Warfarin inhibits vitamin K recycling; vitamin K deficiency typically prolongs PT first because factor VII has a short half-life.
Vitamins A and D can cause important toxicity because they are stored; high-dose vitamin A is teratogenic.

traps.wrong: Vitamin K is needed to synthesize the peptide chains of clotting factors.
traps.right: It enables post-translational γ-carboxylation so selected factors can bind Ca2+.

traps.wrong: The kidney performs the first hydroxylation of vitamin D.
traps.right: The liver makes 25-OH D first; the kidney then makes active 1,25-(OH)2 D.

recognition: Night blindness is the earliest classic vitamin A clue.
Hemolytic anemia with neurologic dysfunction in fat malabsorption suggests vitamin E deficiency.
Bleeding in a newborn or after prolonged antibiotics suggests vitamin K deficiency.

source.label: TUMS Vitamin lecture + Lippincott
source.detail: Vitamin 2024.pdf, pp. 46–70; Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, Chapter 28.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.topic: Fatty acids, storage, oxidation, and eicosanoids
lessons.title: Fatty acids: from structure to fuel and signals
lessons.subtitle: Read saturation, storage, β-oxidation, and eicosanoid origin together

visual.caption: Fatty-acid structure determines packing; nutritional state determines storage, oxidation, or signaling use.

items.label: Structure
items.detail: Saturated chains pack tightly; cis double bonds create kinks and lower melting point. Omega numbering begins at the methyl end.

items.label: Storage
items.detail: Three fatty acyl chains esterified to glycerol form neutral triacylglycerol, stored without water in lipid droplets.

items.label: Mobilization
items.detail: Lipases release free fatty acids, which circulate bound to albumin and are activated to fatty acyl-CoA.

items.label: β-oxidation
items.detail: Repeated mitochondrial oxidation, hydration, oxidation, and thiolysis shorten the chain by two carbons, producing acetyl-CoA, NADH, and FADH2.

items.label: Eicosanoids
items.detail: Arachidonic acid released from membrane phospholipids forms prostaglandins/thromboxanes via cyclooxygenase and leukotrienes via lipoxygenase.

essentials: Long-chain fatty acids require the carnitine shuttle to enter the mitochondrial matrix for β-oxidation.
Each β-oxidation cycle removes one acetyl-CoA and generates one NADH and one FADH2, except the final cleavage yields two acetyl-CoA.
Triacylglycerols are nonpolar storage lipids; phospholipids are amphipathic structural lipids.
Aspirin and other NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase products, not leukotriene synthesis.

traps.wrong: Cis double bonds allow tighter fatty-acid packing.
traps.right: Cis double bonds introduce kinks, reduce packing, and increase fluidity.

traps.wrong: β-oxidation directly generates glucose from even-chain fatty acids.
traps.right: Even-chain fatty acids generate acetyl-CoA, which cannot yield net glucose in humans.

recognition: A kinked hydrocarbon chain usually represents a cis unsaturated fatty acid.
A glycerol backbone with three esterified fatty acids is triacylglycerol.
Arachidonic acid plus COX points to prostaglandins or thromboxanes; 5-LOX points to leukotrienes.

source.label: TUMS Lipid structure + Lippincott
source.detail: Lipid structure Esmaeili.pdf, fatty-acid, triacylglycerol, and eicosanoid sections; Lippincott lipid chemistry cross-check.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Recognizing lipid classes by backbone and head group
lessons.subtitle: Glycerol versus sphingosine is the fastest route to the answer

visual.caption: Identify the backbone first, then phosphate versus carbohydrate head group.

items.label: Glycerophospholipid
items.detail: Glycerol + two fatty acids + phosphate + polar alcohol; examples include phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylethanolamine, and cardiolipin.

items.label: Ceramide
items.detail: Sphingosine backbone plus one amide-linked fatty acid; this is the core of sphingolipids.

items.label: Sphingomyelin
items.detail: Ceramide plus phosphocholine; it is both a sphingolipid and a phospholipid and is abundant in myelin.

items.label: Cerebroside
items.detail: Ceramide plus one sugar and no phosphate; neutral glycosphingolipid.

items.label: Ganglioside
items.detail: Ceramide plus an oligosaccharide containing sialic acid; negatively charged glycosphingolipid.

essentials: Most membrane lipids are amphipathic: polar heads face water while hydrophobic tails form the bilayer core.
Phosphatidylinositol derivatives participate in intracellular signaling; cardiolipin is characteristic of the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Phosphatidylcholine, also called lecithin, is a major membrane phospholipid and pulmonary surfactant component.
Glycosphingolipids contribute to cell recognition and blood-group antigens on the outer membrane leaflet.

traps.wrong: All phospholipids have glycerol backbones.
traps.right: Sphingomyelin is a phospholipid built on ceramide rather than glycerol.

traps.wrong: Cerebrosides contain phosphate.
traps.right: Cerebrosides are ceramide plus one sugar and contain no phosphate.

recognition: A long-chain amino alcohol backbone identifies sphingosine.
A negatively charged oligosaccharide containing sialic acid identifies a ganglioside.
Two acyl chains on glycerol plus phosphate identifies a glycerophospholipid.

source.label: TUMS Lipid structure
source.detail: Lipid structure Esmaeili.pdf, lipid classification, phospholipid, sphingolipid, and membrane sections.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Cholesterol and lipoprotein routes
lessons.subtitle: Track dietary lipid, liver lipid, remnants, and reverse transport

visual.caption: Separate the exogenous, endogenous, and reverse-cholesterol pathways.

items.label: Chylomicron
items.detail: Intestine packages dietary TAG with apoB-48; apoC-II activates capillary LPL; apoE directs the remnant to liver.

items.label: VLDL
items.detail: Liver exports endogenous TAG with apoB-100; LPL removes TAG, producing IDL.

items.label: IDL
items.detail: VLDL remnant either returns to liver through apoE or loses more TAG to become LDL.

items.label: LDL
items.detail: Cholesterol-rich particle delivers cholesterol to cells through LDL receptors recognizing apoB-100.

items.label: HDL
items.detail: Collects peripheral cholesterol; apoA-I activates LCAT, supporting reverse cholesterol transport to liver.

essentials: Cholesterol is a membrane component and precursor of steroid hormones, bile acids, and vitamin D; it is not oxidized for energy.
Lipoprotein density rises as protein proportion rises: chylomicron < VLDL < IDL < LDL < HDL.
ApoC-II activates lipoprotein lipase; apoE mediates remnant uptake; apoB-100 binds the LDL receptor; apoB-48 is structural in chylomicrons.
Free cholesterol is amphipathic at the surface; cholesteryl ester is hydrophobic and stored in the particle core.

traps.wrong: LDL transports dietary triacylglycerol from the intestine.
traps.right: Chylomicrons carry dietary TAG; LDL chiefly delivers cholesterol.

traps.wrong: ApoC-II is the ligand for hepatic remnant uptake.
traps.right: ApoC-II activates LPL; apoE mediates remnant uptake.

recognition: Largest, least dense, TAG-rich particle after a meal: chylomicron.
A cholesterol-rich apoB-100 particle binding peripheral receptors: LDL.
ApoA-I plus LCAT and cholesterol retrieval: HDL.

source.label: TUMS Lipid structure + Lippincott
source.detail: Lipid structure Esmaeili.pdf, cholesterol and lipoprotein sections; Lippincott lipoprotein cross-check.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Amino acids: charge, pI, and side-chain logic
lessons.subtitle: Use pH versus pKa to predict charge and behavior

visual.caption: The common backbone gives acid-base behavior; the R group gives chemical identity.

items.label: Common backbone
items.detail: An α-carbon bears amino, carboxyl, hydrogen, and R groups; glycine is achiral because R is H.

items.label: Low pH
items.detail: Ionizable groups are more protonated and net charge becomes more positive.

items.label: Isoelectric point
items.detail: At pI, average net charge is zero and electrophoretic movement is minimal.

items.label: High pH
items.detail: Ionizable groups are more deprotonated and net charge becomes more negative.

items.label: Side chains
items.detail: Nonpolar, polar uncharged, acidic, basic, aromatic, sulfur-containing, and branched-chain categories predict interactions.

essentials: At physiological pH, free amino acids usually exist as zwitterions with NH3+ and COO− groups.
Acidic side chains are Asp and Glu; basic side chains are Lys, Arg, and His.
The peptide bond is planar and has partial double-bond character, restricting rotation.
Essential amino acids must be supplied in the diet; conditionally essential amino acids become limiting in growth or illness.

traps.wrong: At pH below its pI, an amino acid has a net negative charge.
traps.right: Below pI it is more protonated and net positive; above pI it is net negative.

traps.wrong: Every amino acid is optically active.
traps.right: Glycine is achiral because it has two hydrogens attached to its α-carbon.

recognition: A sulfur-containing side chain that can form disulfides is cysteine.
An imidazole side chain with a pKa near physiological pH is histidine.
A cyclic side chain bonded to the amino nitrogen identifies proline.

source.label: TUMS Amino acids and Proteins
source.detail: Amino acids and Proteins.Part1.pdf, amino-acid structure, classification, ionization, and peptide-bond sections.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Protein structure: four levels and what denaturation breaks
lessons.subtitle: Match every structural level to its stabilizing interactions

visual.caption: Each higher level depends on the sequence below it and adds new interactions.

items.label: Primary
items.detail: Linear amino-acid sequence joined by covalent peptide bonds; ultimately specifies folding information.

items.label: Secondary
items.detail: Local α-helices, β-sheets, and turns stabilized mainly by backbone hydrogen bonds.

items.label: Tertiary
items.detail: Three-dimensional fold of one polypeptide stabilized by hydrophobic packing, hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, van der Waals forces, and sometimes disulfides.

items.label: Quaternary
items.detail: Arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits, as in hemoglobin.

items.label: Denaturation
items.detail: Heat, extreme pH, detergents, or solvents disrupt higher-order structure and function without normally hydrolyzing peptide bonds.

essentials: Hydrophobic side chains tend to be buried in soluble globular proteins, while polar groups tend to face water.
Proline disrupts α-helices; glycine increases flexibility; disulfides are covalent links between cysteines.
Denaturation usually destroys secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structure while preserving primary structure.
Molecular chaperones assist folding and prevent aggregation but do not dictate the amino-acid sequence.

traps.wrong: Denaturation cleaves peptide bonds and changes primary structure.
traps.right: Ordinary denaturation disrupts noncovalent folding interactions, not peptide-bond sequence.

traps.wrong: α-helices are stabilized mainly by side-chain hydrogen bonds.
traps.right: Their repeating hydrogen bonds are between peptide-backbone C=O and N–H groups.

recognition: A repeated coiled ribbon is an α-helix; aligned arrows usually depict a β-sheet.
Several differently colored subunits assembled together depict quaternary structure.

source.label: TUMS Amino acids and Proteins
source.detail: Amino acids and Proteins.Part1.pdf, peptide and protein structure, folding, and denaturation sections.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Michaelis–Menten kinetics
lessons.subtitle: Read Km and Vmax from curves and experimental changes

visual.caption: Substrate binding produces ES; catalysis releases product and regenerates free enzyme.

items.label: Binding
items.detail: E + S ⇌ ES; increasing substrate raises ES formation and initial velocity.

items.label: Low substrate
items.detail: Velocity is approximately proportional to substrate concentration because many active sites are free.

items.label: Km point
items.detail: When [S] = Km, velocity equals one-half Vmax for a Michaelis–Menten enzyme.

items.label: Saturation
items.detail: At high substrate, nearly all active sites are occupied and velocity approaches Vmax.

items.label: More enzyme
items.detail: Adding enzyme raises Vmax proportionally but does not change Km when other conditions remain constant.

essentials: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]).
Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax and often inversely reflects affinity, but only under the model’s assumptions.
Vmax depends on total enzyme concentration; kcat = Vmax/[E]total.
A Michaelis–Menten plot is hyperbolic; many allosteric enzymes show a sigmoidal velocity curve.

traps.wrong: A larger Km always means greater substrate affinity.
traps.right: For simple kinetics, a smaller Km generally means half-maximal velocity is reached at less substrate and suggests greater affinity.

traps.wrong: Adding more enzyme lowers Km.
traps.right: Adding enzyme raises Vmax; Km is unchanged.

recognition: The substrate concentration at half the plateau is Km.
On a Lineweaver–Burk plot, y-intercept = 1/Vmax and x-intercept = −1/Km.

source.label: TUMS Enzyme Kinetics
source.detail: Enzyme Kinetics and regulation- Session2 2024.pptx, Michaelis–Menten and Lineweaver–Burk sections.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Enzyme inhibition and control
lessons.subtitle: Predict Km/Vmax changes, then identify the regulatory strategy

visual.caption: First ask where the inhibitor binds; then ask whether extra substrate can overcome it.

items.label: Competitive
items.detail: Binds free enzyme at the active site; apparent Km rises, Vmax is unchanged, and high substrate can overcome inhibition.

items.label: Pure noncompetitive
items.detail: Binds E and ES equally at a separate site; Vmax falls while Km remains unchanged.

items.label: Uncompetitive
items.detail: Binds only ES; both apparent Km and Vmax fall by the same factor.

items.label: Mixed
items.detail: Binds E and ES unequally; Vmax falls and Km may rise or fall.

items.label: Physiologic control
items.detail: Allostery is rapid and reversible; phosphorylation is covalent and reversible; zymogen cleavage is irreversible; enzyme amount changes slowly.

essentials: Competitive inhibitors produce intersecting Lineweaver–Burk lines at the y-axis because 1/Vmax is unchanged.
Pure noncompetitive lines intersect at the x-axis because Km is unchanged; uncompetitive lines are parallel.
Feedback inhibition usually targets an early committed step, preventing unnecessary synthesis of an end product.
Allosteric enzymes often have multiple subunits, cooperative behavior, and sigmoidal kinetics.

traps.wrong: All noncompetitive inhibition changes Km.
traps.right: Pure noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax without changing Km; mixed inhibition changes both.

traps.wrong: Phosphorylation always activates enzymes.
traps.right: Phosphorylation can activate or inhibit, depending on the enzyme and pathway.

recognition: Same Vmax but a right-shifted saturation curve indicates competitive inhibition.
Parallel Lineweaver–Burk lines indicate uncompetitive inhibition.
A secreted inactive digestive precursor activated by cleavage is a zymogen.

source.label: TUMS Enzyme Kinetics and Regulation
source.detail: Enzyme Kinetics and regulation- Session2 2024.pptx, inhibition, allostery, covalent regulation, and zymogen sections.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Nucleotides, DNA helices, and melting
lessons.subtitle: Build DNA from base to helix and recognize A-, B-, and Z-DNA

visual.caption: DNA structure builds in layers: base → nucleoside → nucleotide → strand → double helix.

items.label: Base
items.detail: Purines are adenine and guanine; pyrimidines are cytosine, thymine, and uracil.

items.label: Nucleoside
items.detail: Nitrogenous base linked to ribose or deoxyribose by a β-N-glycosidic bond; no phosphate.

items.label: Nucleotide
items.detail: Nucleoside plus one or more phosphate groups; polymerization forms 3′–5′ phosphodiester bonds.

items.label: B-DNA
items.detail: Predominant physiological form: right-handed, antiparallel strands with major and minor grooves; A pairs T and G pairs C.

items.label: Melting
items.detail: Heat or extreme pH disrupts hydrogen bonding and base stacking, separates strands, and increases absorbance at 260 nm.

essentials: A–T has two hydrogen bonds and G–C has three; higher GC content generally raises melting temperature.
The two DNA strands run antiparallel, one 5′→3′ and the other 3′→5′.
B-DNA is right-handed and common; A-DNA is shorter and wider; Z-DNA is left-handed with a zigzag backbone.
Denaturation separates strands without breaking the covalent phosphodiester backbone; slow cooling can permit renaturation.

traps.wrong: A nucleoside contains a phosphate group.
traps.right: A nucleoside is base plus sugar; adding phosphate makes a nucleotide.

traps.wrong: DNA melting hydrolyzes phosphodiester bonds.
traps.right: Melting disrupts noncovalent base pairing and stacking while strands remain covalently intact.

recognition: A left-handed helix with a zigzag backbone identifies Z-DNA.
An increase in A260 during heating is the hyperchromic effect of DNA denaturation.
A five-membered plus six-membered fused ring is a purine.

source.label: TUMS DNA Structure
source.detail: Deoxyribonucleic Acid(DNA)Structure (2).pdf, nucleotide, helix conformation, and denaturation sections.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Chromatin: packing DNA while controlling access
lessons.subtitle: From nucleosome core to active and silent domains

visual.caption: DNA accessibility changes as the fiber is wrapped, linked, looped, and chemically marked.

items.label: DNA double helix
items.detail: Negatively charged phosphate backbone is attracted to positively charged lysine- and arginine-rich histones.

items.label: Nucleosome core
items.detail: About 147 base pairs wrap around an octamer containing two each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4.

items.label: Linker
items.detail: Linker DNA connects nucleosomes; histone H1 binds the linker region and promotes higher-order compaction.

items.label: Euchromatin
items.detail: Relatively open, lightly staining, and generally transcriptionally active.

items.label: Heterochromatin
items.detail: Condensed, dark, and generally transcriptionally silent; may be constitutive or facultative.

essentials: Core histones are H2A, H2B, H3, and H4; H1 is a linker histone, not part of the core octamer.
Histone acetylation neutralizes lysine charge, often opens chromatin, and correlates with transcriptional activation.
Promoter CpG DNA methylation commonly correlates with transcriptional repression.
ATP-dependent chromatin-remodeling complexes reposition or eject nucleosomes to alter DNA access.

traps.wrong: Histone H1 is one of the four proteins duplicated in the nucleosome core.
traps.right: The core contains H2A, H2B, H3, and H4; H1 binds linker DNA.

traps.wrong: Histone acetylation usually condenses chromatin.
traps.right: Acetylation usually reduces histone–DNA attraction and favors open, active chromatin.

recognition: Beads on a string depict nucleosomes joined by linker DNA.
A dark condensed nuclear region is heterochromatin; a pale dispersed region is euchromatin.

source.label: TUMS DNA Structure
source.detail: Deoxyribonucleic Acid(DNA)Structure (2).pdf, histone, nucleosome, and chromatin-packing sections.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: DNA replication fork and the chromosome-end problem
lessons.subtitle: Assign every enzyme to its exact job and direction

visual.caption: The fork opens once, but both new strands are synthesized only 5′→3′.

items.label: Open
items.detail: Helicase separates parental strands; single-strand binding proteins stabilize them; topoisomerase relieves torsional stress ahead of the fork.

items.label: Prime
items.detail: Primase makes a short RNA primer because DNA polymerases require an existing 3′-OH.

items.label: Extend
items.detail: DNA polymerase reads template 3′→5′ and synthesizes new DNA 5′→3′.

items.label: Continuous vs fragments
items.detail: Leading synthesis follows the fork continuously; lagging synthesis forms Okazaki fragments away from the fork.

items.label: Finish
items.detail: RNA primers are removed and replaced; ligase seals nicks. Telomerase extends chromosome ends using its internal RNA template.

essentials: Replication is semiconservative: each daughter duplex contains one parental and one newly synthesized strand.
DNA polymerase proofreading is typically 3′→5′ exonuclease activity, opposite the direction of synthesis.
In eukaryotes, DNA polymerase α initiates with primase, polymerase ε mainly extends leading DNA, and polymerase δ mainly extends lagging DNA.
Telomerase is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase active in germ cells, stem cells, and many cancers but low in most somatic cells.

traps.wrong: The lagging strand is synthesized 3′→5′.
traps.right: Both strands are synthesized 5′→3′; lagging synthesis is discontinuous because of template orientation.

traps.wrong: DNA ligase synthesizes Okazaki fragments.
traps.right: DNA polymerase synthesizes the fragments; ligase seals the remaining phosphodiester nicks.

recognition: Short discontinuous segments with repeated primers identify the lagging strand.
An enzyme with an internal RNA template extending a 3′ chromosome end is telomerase.
Positive supercoiling ahead of a fork is relieved by topoisomerase.

source.label: TUMS DNA Replication
source.detail: Deoxyribonucleic Acid(DNA Replication (1).pptx, replication machinery, proofreading, termination, and telomere sections.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: RNA and transcription
lessons.subtitle: Choose the polymerase, direction, processing step, and inhibitor

visual.caption: Transcription makes RNA 5′→3′, then eukaryotic pre-mRNA is capped, spliced, and polyadenylated.

items.label: Promoter recognition
items.detail: Transcription factors and RNA polymerase assemble at a promoter; no RNA primer is required.

items.label: Elongation
items.detail: Polymerase reads the DNA template strand 3′→5′ while synthesizing RNA 5′→3′.

items.label: 5′ cap
items.detail: 7-methylguanosine protects mRNA and supports nuclear export and translation initiation.

items.label: Splicing
items.detail: The spliceosome removes introns, usually joining exons at GU–AG boundaries through a lariat intermediate.

items.label: 3′ poly(A)
items.detail: Cleavage after the AAUAAA signal is followed by polyadenylation, improving stability, export, and translation.

essentials: RNA polymerase I makes most rRNA; II makes mRNA and several regulatory RNAs; III makes tRNA and 5S rRNA.
The RNA sequence matches the coding DNA strand except U replaces T; it is complementary to the template strand.
RNA differs from DNA by ribose 2′-OH, uracil instead of thymine, and usually single-stranded structure.
Rifampin inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase; α-amanitin strongly inhibits eukaryotic RNA polymerase II; actinomycin D intercalates DNA and blocks transcription.

traps.wrong: RNA polymerase requires a primer with a free 3′-OH.
traps.right: RNA polymerase initiates de novo; DNA polymerase requires a primer.

traps.wrong: The poly(A) tail is encoded directly as a long DNA thymidine tract.
traps.right: The transcript is cleaved after a signal, then poly(A) polymerase adds the tail without a DNA template.

recognition: A 5′–5′ triphosphate-linked methylguanosine is the mRNA cap.
A lariat with a 2′–5′ bond identifies pre-mRNA splicing.
A toxin selectively blocking eukaryotic mRNA synthesis points to α-amanitin.

source.label: TUMS Transcription
source.detail: Transcription 2025.pptx, RNA types, polymerases, processing, and inhibitor sections.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Gene regulation: lac, trp, and eukaryotic control
lessons.subtitle: Inducible catabolism, repressible synthesis, and chromatin-based regulation

visual.caption: The lac operon turns on substrate breakdown; the trp operon turns off product synthesis.

items.label: lac: no lactose
items.detail: Active repressor binds the operator and blocks transcription.

items.label: lac: lactose present
items.detail: Allolactose inactivates the repressor; expression is highest when glucose is also low, allowing high cAMP–CAP activation.

items.label: trp: tryptophan low
items.detail: Repressor lacks corepressor and the ribosome stalls in the leader, favoring antitermination and transcription of biosynthetic genes.

items.label: trp: tryptophan high
items.detail: Tryptophan activates the repressor and permits attenuation-mediated termination.

items.label: Eukaryotes
items.detail: Chromatin state, transcription factors, enhancers/silencers, RNA processing, RNA stability, translation, and protein modification all regulate expression.

essentials: lac is an inducible catabolic operon under both negative control by repressor and positive control by cAMP–CAP.
Glucose lowers cAMP; therefore high glucose prevents maximal lac expression even when lactose is present.
trp is a repressible anabolic operon; tryptophan acts as a corepressor and also influences attenuation.
Enhancers can act at a distance and in either orientation through DNA looping and transcription-factor recruitment.

traps.wrong: Lactose directly activates CAP.
traps.right: Allolactose inactivates the repressor; low glucose raises cAMP, which activates CAP.

traps.wrong: High tryptophan induces the trp biosynthetic operon.
traps.right: High tryptophan represses and attenuates the operon because the product is already abundant.

recognition: Maximum lac expression requires lactose present and glucose absent or low.
A leader peptide with adjacent terminator/antiterminator hairpins indicates attenuation.
Open acetylated chromatin near an enhancer suggests active eukaryotic transcription.

source.label: TUMS Regulation of Gene Expression
source.detail: Regulation of Gene Expression 2025.pptx, lac operon, trp operon, attenuation, and eukaryotic regulation sections.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Translation and mutation consequences
lessons.subtitle: Move from codon recognition to protein synthesis, then predict what sequence changes do

visual.caption: Translation reads mRNA 5′→3′ and builds protein from amino terminus to carboxyl terminus.

items.label: Charge tRNA
items.detail: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases use ATP to attach the correct amino acid to its tRNA and provide major fidelity.

items.label: Initiate
items.detail: Small subunit finds AUG; initiator Met-tRNA occupies the P site; the large subunit joins.

items.label: Elongate
items.detail: Aminoacyl-tRNA enters A, rRNA catalyzes peptide-bond transfer to the A-site chain, then translocation moves tRNAs A→P→E.
items.cue: A arrives, P holds, E exits

items.label: Terminate
items.detail: A stop codon recruits a release factor rather than tRNA, hydrolyzing and releasing the completed polypeptide.

items.label: Mutation effect
items.detail: Substitution may be silent, missense, or nonsense; an insertion/deletion not divisible by three shifts the downstream reading frame.

essentials: The genetic code is degenerate but unambiguous: multiple codons may specify one amino acid, but each codon specifies only one amino acid.
Peptidyl transferase activity is catalytic rRNA in the large ribosomal subunit, making the ribosome a ribozyme.
Bacterial 70S ribosomes contain 30S and 50S subunits; eukaryotic 80S ribosomes contain 40S and 60S subunits.
Tetracyclines block aminoacyl-tRNA entry to bacterial 30S; chloramphenicol blocks 50S peptidyl transferase; macrolides block 50S translocation; diphtheria toxin inhibits eukaryotic eEF-2.

traps.wrong: The growing peptide is synthesized from C-terminus to N-terminus.
traps.right: New amino acids are added to the C-terminus, so synthesis proceeds N→C.

traps.wrong: Every base substitution changes an amino acid.
traps.right: Code degeneracy permits silent substitutions; others may be missense or nonsense.

recognition: A premature stop codon is a nonsense mutation.
An insertion of one or two bases produces a frameshift; an insertion of three bases is in-frame.
A toxin ADP-ribosylating eEF-2 points to diphtheria toxin or exotoxin A.

source.label: TUMS Translation
source.detail: Translation 2025.pptx, genetic code, tRNA/ribosome, synthesis stages, mutation effects, and inhibitor sections.

lessons.subject: biochemistry
lessons.title: Practical biochemistry: equipment, titration, and carbohydrate tests
lessons.subtitle: Recognize the tool, reaction principle, positive result, and selectivity

visual.caption: For each practical station, name what is detected, the positive appearance, and the important limitation.

items.label: Molisch
items.detail: General carbohydrate test: dehydration forms furfural derivatives that react with α-naphthol, producing a violet ring at the interface.

items.label: Benedict
items.detail: Reducing sugars reduce Cu2+ in alkaline solution; color progresses from blue through green/yellow/orange to brick-red precipitate with increasing reduction.

items.label: Barfoed and Seliwanoff
items.detail: Barfoed rapidly favors monosaccharides in acidic copper reagent; Seliwanoff rapidly produces cherry-red color with ketoses, especially ketohexoses.

items.label: Iodine
items.detail: Iodine fits the amylose helix to produce blue-black color; heating disrupts the complex and cooling can restore it.

items.label: Volumetric work
items.detail: Burette delivers variable measured volume; volumetric pipette transfers one precise volume; volumetric flask prepares one precise final volume; titration uses N1V1 = N2V2 at stoichiometric equivalence.

essentials: Read the bottom of a colorless meniscus at eye level and remove air bubbles from a burette tip before titration.
A titration endpoint is the indicator color change; the equivalence point is the stoichiometric chemical point, and they should be close but are not identical concepts.
Phenolphthalein is colorless in acid and pink in sufficiently basic solution; use the first persistent faint pink endpoint, not a dark overshoot.
Analytical balances require draft protection; fume hoods protect from hazardous vapors; centrifuges must be balanced with opposing equal masses.
Sucrose is nonreducing before hydrolysis but its monosaccharide products are reducing.

traps.wrong: Benedict distinguishes glucose specifically from every other sugar.
traps.right: Benedict detects reducing ability and is not glucose-specific.

traps.wrong: A volumetric flask is used to dispense many precise variable volumes.
traps.right: It is calibrated to contain one precise final volume; a burette delivers variable measured volumes.

traps.wrong: Seliwanoff is a general test for all carbohydrates.
traps.right: Molisch is general; Seliwanoff distinguishes ketoses by their faster cherry-red reaction.

recognition: A long graduated tube with a stopcock is a burette.
A bulb-centered pipette with one calibration mark is a volumetric pipette.
A narrow-neck flask with one calibration line is a volumetric flask.
A violet ring at a liquid interface is a positive Molisch test.

source.label: TUMS Practical Biochemistry
source.detail: Carbohydrate Qualification Test Esmaeili Jan 2026.pdf; Laboratory Equipment Esmaeili Jan 2026.pdf; Titration Esmaeili Jan 2026.pdf.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Cell physiology and homeostatic control
lessons.subtitle: Internal environment, feedback loops, and membrane organization

visual.caption: A homeostatic system detects a deviation, compares it with a target, and drives an opposing response.

items.label: Controlled variable
items.detail: A physiologic quantity such as temperature, pressure, glucose, pH, or osmolarity is maintained within a useful range.

items.label: Sensor
items.detail: A receptor detects the current value or change and sends input to an integrating center.

items.label: Integrator
items.detail: Compares input with the desired state and generates an output command.

items.label: Effector
items.detail: Changes organ function so negative feedback reduces the initiating error.

items.label: Cell boundary
items.detail: The lipid bilayer, membrane proteins, and glycocalyx control exchange, signaling, adhesion, and identity between ICF and ECF.

essentials: ECF is the body’s internal environment; stable ECF composition supports cell function despite external change.
Negative feedback is stabilizing and most common; positive feedback amplifies a process and requires a terminating event, as in clotting or childbirth.
Feedback gain describes correction relative to remaining error; a larger absolute negative gain means more effective control.
Pinocytosis internalizes fluid and small solutes; phagocytosis engulfs large particles; lysosomes digest endocytosed material; exocytosis releases vesicular contents.

traps.wrong: Positive feedback always causes disease and has no normal role.
traps.right: It serves normal processes such as labor, clotting, and the explosive upstroke of an action potential, but needs an endpoint.

traps.wrong: Homeostasis means physiologic variables never change.
traps.right: They fluctuate within regulated ranges around functional targets.

recognition: A response that reverses the initial change is negative feedback.
A response that reinforces the initial change until a defined endpoint is positive feedback.
Engulfment of a bacterium by pseudopods is phagocytosis.

source.label: TUMS Cell Physiology + Guyton
source.detail: Introduction to Cell Physiology PDF.pdf, pp. 1–4; Guyton and Hall, 15th ed., Chapters 1–2.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Membrane transport: diffusion, carriers, pumps, and osmosis
lessons.subtitle: Classify transport by protein use, energy source, direction, and saturation

visual.caption: Determine whether movement follows the electrochemical gradient and where its energy comes from.

items.label: Simple diffusion
items.detail: Moves down a gradient through lipid or an open channel without metabolic energy; flux rises with gradient and permeability.

items.label: Facilitated diffusion
items.detail: Carrier-mediated downhill movement; selective, competitively inhibitable, and saturable at a transport maximum.

items.label: Primary active
items.detail: A pump directly hydrolyzes ATP to move solute uphill, as Na+/K+-ATPase, Ca2+-ATPase, and H+/K+-ATPase do.

items.label: Secondary active
items.detail: Uphill movement of one solute is coupled to downhill movement of another whose gradient was created by primary transport.

items.label: Osmosis
items.detail: Water crosses toward higher effective osmolarity; aquaporins increase water permeability.

essentials: Na+/K+-ATPase moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP, maintains ion gradients, and is directly electrogenic.
Na+–glucose cotransport is symport; Na+/Ca2+ and Na+/H+ exchange are antiport examples.
Channels can be voltage-, ligand-, or mechanically gated; carriers bind solute and undergo conformational cycling.
Tonicity predicts sustained cell-volume change and depends on nonpenetrating solutes, not every measured osmole.

traps.wrong: Facilitated diffusion can move a solute against its electrochemical gradient.
traps.right: It is passive and moves downhill; active transport is required for net uphill movement.

traps.wrong: Secondary active transport directly hydrolyzes ATP at its carrier.
traps.right: It uses an ion gradient established indirectly by an ATP-driven primary pump.

recognition: A velocity curve approaching Vmax identifies carrier saturation.
A transporter moving Na+ and glucose in the same direction is a symporter.
A 3-out/2-in pump diagram identifies Na+/K+-ATPase.

source.label: TUMS Cell Physiology + Guyton
source.detail: Introduction to Cell Physiology PDF.pdf, pp. 5–9; Guyton and Hall, 15th ed., Chapter 4.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Resting membrane potential and equilibrium potentials
lessons.subtitle: Separate ion gradients, permeability, and the electrogenic pump

visual.caption: A concentration gradient starts ion movement; charge separation creates an opposing electrical gradient.

items.label: Gradient
items.detail: Na+ is concentrated outside and K+ inside, mainly because Na+/K+-ATPase continuously maintains these distributions.

items.label: Selective permeability
items.detail: At rest, many cells are far more permeable to K+ than Na+ because of K+ leak channels.

items.label: K+ efflux
items.detail: K+ diffuses outward, leaving impermeant negative charges behind and making the cell interior negative.

items.label: Electrical opposition
items.detail: The negative interior attracts K+ inward until electrical and chemical driving forces balance at EK.

items.label: Actual resting value
items.detail: Small Na+ permeability shifts Vm positive from EK; the electrogenic 3:2 pump contributes a few additional negative millivolts.

essentials: The Nernst equation gives the equilibrium potential for one ion; the Goldman equation combines multiple permeant ions and their relative permeabilities.
Increasing extracellular K+ reduces the K+ gradient, makes EK less negative, and usually depolarizes the membrane.
Depolarization means Vm becomes less negative; hyperpolarization means it becomes more negative.
Driving force depends on Vm − Eion; an ion has no net flux through open channels when Vm equals its equilibrium potential.

traps.wrong: The Na+/K+ pump directly creates the entire resting membrane potential.
traps.right: Selective K+ leak is the main immediate cause; the pump maintains gradients and adds a small electrogenic effect.

traps.wrong: At an ion’s equilibrium potential, the ion stops moving microscopically.
traps.right: Movement continues in both directions, but net electrochemical flux is zero.

recognition: A membrane potential near EK indicates dominant K+ permeability.
Acute hyperkalemia usually shifts resting potential in a depolarizing direction.
A calculation involving only one ion calls for Nernst; several ions call for Goldman.

source.label: TUMS Cell Physiology + Guyton
source.detail: Introduction to Cell Physiology PDF.pdf, pp. 9–10; Guyton and Hall, 15th ed., Chapter 5.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Action potentials: gates, phases, propagation, and refractoriness
lessons.subtitle: Follow Na+ activation, Na+ inactivation, delayed K+ opening, and recovery

visual.caption: The waveform is the visible result of time-dependent channel-state changes.

items.label: Rest
items.detail: Voltage-gated Na+ activation gates are closed, inactivation gates are open, and delayed K+ channels are mostly closed.

items.label: Threshold and upstroke
items.detail: Na+ activation gates open rapidly; Na+ influx causes regenerative depolarization and an all-or-none spike.

items.label: Peak
items.detail: Na+ channels inactivate while delayed K+ channels open, terminating the upstroke.

items.label: Repolarization
items.detail: K+ efflux returns Vm negative; persistent K+ conductance can cause after-hyperpolarization.

items.label: Recovery
items.detail: Na+ channels recover from inactivation as Vm repolarizes; K+ channels close slowly, restoring full excitability.

essentials: During the absolute refractory period, most Na+ channels are inactivated and no second propagated action potential can occur.
During the relative refractory period, some Na+ channels have recovered but elevated K+ conductance means a stronger stimulus is required.
Action-potential amplitude does not encode stimulus strength; frequency and recruited fibers do.
Myelin increases membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, allowing saltatory regeneration at nodes of Ranvier with faster, more efficient conduction.
Plateau action potentials reflect prolonged inward Ca2+ current plus reduced or delayed K+ efflux.

traps.wrong: Repolarization occurs because Na+/K+-ATPase rapidly pumps out the entering Na+.
traps.right: Rapid repolarization is mainly caused by Na+ channel inactivation and opening of voltage-gated K+ channels.

traps.wrong: A stronger suprathreshold stimulus makes one action potential taller.
traps.right: The spike is all-or-none; stronger stimuli generally increase firing frequency.

recognition: The steep rising phase of a nerve action potential indicates rapid voltage-gated Na+ influx.
An impulse jumping between exposed gaps in myelin is saltatory conduction.
A prolonged depolarized phase with L-type Ca2+ entry is a plateau.

source.label: TUMS Cell Physiology + Guyton
source.detail: Introduction to Cell Physiology PDF.pdf, pp. 10–14; Guyton and Hall, 15th ed., Chapter 5.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Skeletal muscle: sarcomere and cross-bridge cycle
lessons.subtitle: Turn filament arrangement into force, shortening, and ATP use

visual.caption: Ca2+ exposes actin sites; ATP controls detachment and recocking; repeated cycles slide thin filaments inward.

items.label: Resting sarcomere
items.detail: Thin actin filaments anchor at Z discs; thick myosin centers at the M line; tropomyosin blocks actin’s myosin-binding sites.

items.label: Expose
items.detail: Ca2+ binds troponin C, shifting tropomyosin away from myosin-binding sites on actin.

items.label: Bind and power stroke
items.detail: Energized myosin–ADP–Pi binds actin; Pi then ADP release drives the head pivot and pulls actin toward the M line.

items.label: Detach
items.detail: A new ATP binds myosin and lowers its affinity for actin, causing detachment.

items.label: Recock
items.detail: Myosin ATPase hydrolyzes ATP to ADP + Pi, returning the head to its high-energy position for another cycle.

essentials: During shortening, I bands and H zones decrease, Z discs approach, but A-band length remains constant because thick filaments do not shorten.
Without ATP, myosin cannot detach from actin, producing rigor; ATP also powers SERCA-mediated Ca2+ reuptake.
Isometric contraction raises tension without shortening; isotonic contraction changes length against an approximately constant load.
Force rises through recruitment of motor units and temporal summation; high-frequency stimulation can produce fused tetanus.
A motor unit is one α-motor neuron and all muscle fibers it innervates; small units permit fine control.

traps.wrong: The A band shortens during contraction.
traps.right: The A band equals thick-filament length and remains constant; I band and H zone narrow.

traps.wrong: ATP binding produces the power stroke.
traps.right: ATP binding detaches myosin; Pi release from the cocked head initiates the power stroke.

recognition: A central thick-filament-only region is the H zone; thin-filament-only regions are I bands.
A force trace rising with repeated stimuli before full relaxation demonstrates temporal summation.
Tension without change in muscle length is isometric contraction.

source.label: TUMS Molecular Basis + Skeletal Muscle
source.detail: 1. Molecular basis of contraction.pdf, pp. 1–24; 2. Skeletal muscle.pdf, pp. 2–7; Guyton and Hall, 15th ed., Chapter 6.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Neuromuscular transmission
lessons.subtitle: From motor-neuron action potential to muscle-fiber threshold

visual.caption: Every NMJ step is ordered: nerve AP → Ca2+ → ACh → end-plate potential → muscle AP → ACh breakdown.

items.label: Nerve terminal depolarizes
items.detail: The motor-neuron action potential opens presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.

items.label: ACh release
items.detail: Ca2+ triggers SNARE-dependent fusion of acetylcholine vesicles with the terminal membrane.

items.label: End-plate current
items.detail: ACh binds muscle nicotinic Nm receptors, opening nonselective cation channels; net Na+ influx generates a graded end-plate potential.

items.label: Muscle action potential
items.detail: Local current reaches adjacent voltage-gated Na+ channels; threshold initiates an all-or-none action potential across sarcolemma and T tubules.

items.label: Terminate
items.detail: Acetylcholinesterase rapidly hydrolyzes ACh; choline is taken back up for resynthesis.

essentials: The end-plate potential is graded and local; the muscle action potential is regenerative and all-or-none.
A normal NMJ has a safety factor: one nerve impulse usually creates an EPP well above muscle threshold.
Myasthenia gravis reduces postsynaptic Nm receptor function; botulinum toxin blocks presynaptic ACh release.
Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors prolong ACh action and can improve transmission in myasthenia, but excess causes cholinergic toxicity.

traps.wrong: The receptor at the skeletal motor end plate is muscarinic.
traps.right: It is a nicotinic Nm ligand-gated cation channel.

traps.wrong: The end-plate potential itself propagates along the entire muscle fiber.
traps.right: The EPP is local; it triggers a propagated voltage-gated muscle action potential.

recognition: Presynaptic vesicles facing deep postsynaptic junctional folds identify the motor end plate.
Fatigable weakness with reduced postsynaptic receptor number points to myasthenia gravis.
Failure of vesicle fusion and ACh release points to botulinum toxin.

source.label: TUMS Skeletal Muscle + Guyton
source.detail: 2. Skeletal muscle.pdf, pp. 8–16 and 21; Guyton and Hall, 15th ed., Chapter 7.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Skeletal excitation–contraction coupling
lessons.subtitle: How a surface action potential releases and then resequesters Ca2+

visual.caption: The action potential travels inward through T tubules so the whole fiber releases Ca2+ nearly together.

items.label: Surface excitation
items.detail: A muscle action potential spreads along the sarcolemma and descends into the fiber through transverse tubules.

items.label: Voltage sensing
items.detail: T-tubule L-type Ca2+ channels called DHP receptors change conformation in response to depolarization.

items.label: SR release
items.detail: Skeletal DHP receptors mechanically open RyR1 channels in adjacent terminal cisternae, releasing stored Ca2+ into cytosol.

items.label: Contraction
items.detail: Cytosolic Ca2+ binds troponin C, moves tropomyosin, and permits cross-bridge cycling.

items.label: Relaxation
items.detail: SERCA pumps Ca2+ back into SR, where calsequestrin binds and stores it; cytosolic Ca2+ falls and tropomyosin reblocks actin.

essentials: A skeletal-muscle triad is one T tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae, typically at the A–I junction.
Skeletal-muscle contraction can occur without extracellular Ca2+ influx for each twitch because DHP mechanically gates SR RyR1.
SERCA consumes ATP directly; calsequestrin permits large Ca2+ storage while keeping free SR Ca2+ lower.
The latent period between action potential and force reflects coupling and cross-bridge activation, not delayed electrical propagation.

traps.wrong: Extracellular Ca2+ entering through DHP is the essential trigger for every skeletal twitch.
traps.right: In skeletal muscle, DHP mainly acts as a voltage sensor mechanically coupled to RyR1; SR Ca2+ supplies the activating pulse.

traps.wrong: Relaxation occurs when Ca2+ is pumped out of the body by Na+/K+-ATPase.
traps.right: SERCA pumps cytosolic Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

recognition: A T tubule between two swollen SR terminal cisternae is a triad.
A membrane voltage sensor directly aligned with an SR release channel depicts DHP–RyR coupling.
An ATP-driven SR membrane pump returning Ca2+ is SERCA.

source.label: TUMS Skeletal Muscle + Guyton
source.detail: 2. Skeletal muscle.pdf, pp. 16–19; 1. Molecular basis of contraction.pdf, pp. 5–12 and 24; Guyton and Hall, 15th ed., Chapter 7.

lessons.subject: physiology
lessons.title: Smooth muscle: calmodulin–MLCK control and economical force
lessons.subtitle: No troponin: regulate myosin, not the thin filament

visual.caption: Smooth muscle raises Ca2+, activates MLCK, phosphorylates myosin, cycles slowly, then relaxes through Ca2+ removal and MLCP.

items.label: Raise Ca2+
items.detail: Depolarization, receptor signaling, stretch, or local factors increase cytosolic Ca2+ from ECF and/or SR stores.

items.label: Calmodulin
items.detail: Ca2+ binds calmodulin because smooth muscle lacks troponin C.

items.label: Activate MLCK
items.detail: Ca2+–calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase, which uses ATP to phosphorylate regulatory myosin light chains.

items.label: Contract
items.detail: Phosphorylated myosin develops ATPase activity and cycles with actin attached to dense bodies; cycling is slow but force can be sustained.

items.label: Relax
items.detail: Ca2+ pumps/exchangers lower cytosolic Ca2+, MLCK becomes inactive, and myosin light-chain phosphatase dephosphorylates myosin.

essentials: Smooth muscle has actin, myosin, tropomyosin, dense bodies, and intermediate filaments but no sarcomeres or troponin, so it is nonstriated.
The latch state maintains force with low ATP consumption after myosin dephosphorylation while some cross-bridges remain attached.
Unitary smooth muscle has gap junctions and coordinated spontaneous or stretch-induced activity; multiunit muscle has more independent fibers and precise neural control.
Autonomic nerve varicosities release transmitter diffusely; receptor subtype determines whether ACh or norepinephrine contracts or relaxes a tissue.
Caveolae are membrane invaginations associated with Ca2+ handling and partially substitute for absent T tubules.

traps.wrong: Ca2+ initiates smooth-muscle contraction by binding troponin C.
traps.right: Smooth muscle lacks troponin; Ca2+ binds calmodulin and activates MLCK.

traps.wrong: Smooth muscle requires an action potential for every contraction.
traps.right: Receptor pathways, stretch, and local chemicals can raise Ca2+ and produce contraction without a propagated action potential.

recognition: Spindle-shaped nonstriated cells with central nuclei identify smooth muscle.
Many gap junctions and spontaneous waves suggest unitary smooth muscle; individually innervated fibers suggest multiunit muscle.
Ca2+–calmodulin → MLCK → myosin phosphorylation is the signature smooth-muscle pathway.

source.label: TUMS Smooth Muscle + Guyton
source.detail: 3. Smooth muscle.pdf, pp. 1–18; Guyton and Hall, 15th ed., Chapter 8.
